guide.title: Handel–Halvorsen: Passacaglia for Violin and Viola – Listening Guide
guide.overview: This is a passacaglia: a short four-measure theme followed by 22 variations, each also four measures long. Early variations stay close to the theme; later ones move far from it. The mood moves from loud and bold to quiet and thoughtful, then to a big, loud finish. Keys and chords here are estimated by computer. The score came from optical recognition and may contain errors, so trust the big picture more than small details.

listening_points.headline: The theme: violin states the pattern boldly
listening_points.text: The violin plays the theme loudly on top, and the viola accompanies below [m. 1-4]. The tune begins by circling around one high note. Learn it. Every variation keeps its four-measure length, and the early ones stay closer to it than the later ones. The key is G minor, which is a darker, serious key.

listening_points.headline: Variation 1: both instruments, still loud
listening_points.text: The two players now share the material as a duet [m. 5-8]. The violin still carries much of the tune. The volume stays loud, then eases off at the end [m. 8].

listening_points.headline: Variations 2–3: softer and more flowing
listening_points.text: The sound drops to a medium-soft level [m. 9-16]. The violin probably leads in Variation 2. In Variation 3 the lead is shared between both players. Listen for swelling and fading within phrases.

listening_points.headline: Variations 4–5: the lead passes to the viola
listening_points.text: Variation 4 starts soft, then gets loud at its end [m. 17-20]. The viola probably takes the lead around [m. 19-22]. Then the violin probably takes over again. Listen for the darker viola voice coming forward.

listening_points.headline: Variations 6–8: busier, quiet playing
listening_points.text: Each bar holds more and more notes, but the volume mostly stays soft [m. 25-36]. The violin mostly seems to lead, though this is less certain in Variation 8. Small swells and sudden accents add drama. It feels like a restless, whispering stretch.

listening_points.headline: Variations 9–10: the players move together
listening_points.text: Here both players often move in the same rhythm, like a hymn [m. 37-43]. This is called homophonic texture. It sounds chordal and warm. The level is soft and then grows to medium loud at [m. 44].

listening_points.headline: Variations 11–12: a hush, with a clearer violin tune
listening_points.text: Variation 11 is a more tangled duet, and neither part clearly leads [m. 45-48]. Then Variation 12 settles into a soft violin melody [m. 49-52]. The violin is easier to follow here.

listening_points.headline: Variation 13: a strong, loud burst
listening_points.text: The music jumps to loud [m. 53-55]. The players sometimes move together in chords and sometimes play separate lines. Then it eases to medium loud at [m. 56].

listening_points.headline: Variations 14–15: the viola probably leads, then a sudden hush
listening_points.text: The viola probably leads here, though this is uncertain [m. 57-62]. The sound drops suddenly from medium loud to very soft at [m. 60] and stays very soft until [m. 63]. Listen for the hush.

listening_points.headline: Variations 16–17: thinning out, soft
listening_points.text: The lead is shared, then the violin comes forward [m. 65-72]. The music gets sparser. By [m. 72] the violin is alone. Briefly the key moves to A minor, which sounds slightly unsettled [m. 71-72].

listening_points.headline: Variation 18: a quiet return, led by the viola
listening_points.text: The score shows two silent measures here [m. 73-74], though this may be a recognition error. The viola then enters alone [m. 75]. The violin joins and the key returns to G minor [m. 75-76].

listening_points.headline: Variation 19: bright major keys, then a loud jump
listening_points.text: The mood brightens in G major, a sunnier version of the home key [m. 77-78]. Then the key moves to F major, and the volume leaps to very loud [m. 79-80]. The violin leads.

listening_points.headline: Variations 20–21: loud, with shifting keys
listening_points.text: The music stays very loud while the key moves around [m. 81-88]. It goes to D minor, which is darker [m. 83-84]. Then it goes to D major, which is brighter [m. 85-87]. The violin leads. The score shows [m. 88] as silent, which may be a recognition error.

listening_points.headline: Variation 22: the loudest point and the ending
listening_points.text: The violin starts alone in G minor, back home [m. 89]. The two players then reach fff, extremely loud, which the computer estimates as the loudest point [m. 90]. The extremely loud playing continues through the last bars [m. 91-93]. The piece ends on a single violin line.

glossary.explanation: A set of variations on a short theme; each variation keeps the theme's length but changes the music.
A new version of the same material. Here each one lasts four measures.
One small unit of musical time, marked off by bar lines. It is also called a bar.
The home note and mood of the music. Minor keys sound darker. Major keys sound brighter.
Both players move together in the same rhythm, like chords.
Both instruments play active, interwoven lines.
A part or the whole ensemble is silent.

glossary.term: Dynamics (pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff, fff)
glossary.explanation: Loudness levels, from very soft (pp) through very loud (ff) to extremely loud (fff).
